name: Mountain Fish Red Peloponnese
text:
## Mountain Fish Red Peloponnese [lcbo-392480]

**A note before we start.** LCBO code 392480 was used for the same wine under the name Mountain Fish Agiorgitiko. On [WineAlign](https://www.winealign.com/wines/71607-Mountain-Fish-Agiorgitiko-2012), that code is tied to the Mountain Fish Agiorgitiko 2012, IGP Peloponnese, at $13.70. That page's bottle image is filed as "Mountain Fish Peloponnese Red", so your listing is the same wine.

Your $6.40 price is about half what the LCBO charged in past years. That points to clearance stock, so check the vintage on the label. I explain why below.

### The region

The grapes come from the mountain fringe of [Nemea](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Nemea,+Corinthia,+Greece&t=k) in the northeastern [Peloponnese](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Peloponnese,+Greece&t=k). The Peloponnese is Greece's largest and most productive wine region, with more than 50 mountains over 1,000 m ([Wines of Greece](https://winesofgreece.org/?p=6964)).

The vineyards are around the villages of Asprokambos and Psari, at about 800 m above sea level ([Le Pont de la Tour](https://www.lepontdelatour.co.uk/whats-on-london-bridge/wine/page/3/)). You can see them from above here: [Psari](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Psari,+Nemea,+Greece&t=k) and [Asprokambos](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Asprokampos,+Nemea,+Greece&t=k).

### The grape

The wine is 100% [Agiorgitiko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Agiorgitiko&go=Go), Greece's leading native red grape. The name comes from Agios Georgios (Saint George), the Byzantine name for the village of Nemea ([Wine with Seth](https://www.winewithseth.com/winewiki/agiorgitiko/)). Locally, Nemea's red is nicknamed the "blood of Hercules", after the lion the hero killed there.

Altitude matters a great deal for this grape. Nemea's mountain zone, 650 to 850 m and including Asprokampos and Psari, gives the appellation's most structured and age-worthy wines. The lower valley floor gives softer, fruitier wines.

### The producer and the name

The label belongs to **Strofilia**. It was made during the years Strofilia was partnered with Katogi Averoff, so older bottles say "Katogi & Strofilia". According to [Wines of Greece](https://winesofgreece.org/?p=4038), Strofilia began in 1980, when two engineer friends, Giannis Maltezos and Achilleas Lampsidis, planted vines on the Maltezos family estate near Anavyssos ([map](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Anavyssos,+Attica,+Greece&t=k)). Treve Ring, writing for [Gismondi on Wine](https://gismondionwine.com/tasting-notes/201705/mountain-fish-agiorgitiko-2014?note=26195), gives the founding year as 1984, so the sources differ.

The partner, Katogi Averoff, comes from [Metsovo](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Metsovo,+Epirus,+Greece&t=k) in the [Pindus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Pindus&go=Go) mountains. The two wineries merged in 2001 but kept their own identities, and the partnership ended in 2016 ([wein.plus](https://glossary.wein.plus/katogi-strofilia)). Recent vintages, such as the 2020 and 2024, carry the Strofilia name alone.

On the name: Psari, the mountain village the wine comes from, means "fish" in Greek ([Waitrose Cellar](https://www.waitrosecellar.com/products/strofilia-mountain-fish-agiorgitiko-705481)). A UK merchant tells it differently: the wine is named after the "mountain fish" living in the stream beside the vineyards ([Hooky](https://www.hooky.co.uk/?p=41915)). Both may be true, since the village likely took its name from the fish.

### How it's made

Treve Ring reports that the grapes grow in deep clay soils and are fermented as whole clusters, with two weeks on the skins and six months in tank before bottling. Waitrose describes it as unoaked, medium-bodied and fruity, with friendly tannins. It is sealed with a screw cap.

### What the reviewers say

**Falstaff, 2016 vintage: 90 points.** Peter Moser rated the 2016 at 90 Falstaff points in 2018 ([Falstaff](https://www.falstaff.com/nordics/wines/strofilia-estate-2016-agiorgitiko-mountain-fish-pgi-peloponnes)). This is the highest score I found. The tasting note is not shown publicly.

**Gismondi on Wine (Treve Ring), 2014 vintage: 88 points.** Tasted in May 2017 and scored 88 points (16/20) ([Gismondi on Wine](https://gismondionwine.com/tasting-notes/201705/mountain-fish-agiorgitiko-2014?note=26195)). In my words: soft, generous plum and dark-cherry fruit, gentle fuzzy tannins and a firm line of acidity. She calls it rustic, charming and good value, and suggests serving it lightly chilled with pork.

**Natalie MacLean, 2013 vintage: 88 points.** She scored the 2013 (LCBO 392480, $11.25) at 88 in August 2016, named it a best-value red, and gave a drinking window of 2014–2017 ([NatalieMacLean.com](https://www.nataliemaclean.com/winepicks/userreviews.aspx?wid=210638)). Her short take is that it is fuller and more savoury than the price suggests, a good match for burgers.

**WineAlign, 2012 and 2013 vintages: 88 and 87 points (aggregate).** The [2012 page](https://www.winealign.com/wines/71607-Mountain-Fish-Agiorgitiko-2012) shows an overall score of 88 from 11 reviews, and 87 for the 2013. Five Canadian critics reviewed the 2012: Sara d'Amato, Steve Thurlow, John Szabo MS, Michael Godel and David Lawrason. Their individual scores are behind a paywall. The public openings of their notes describe it as juicy, lively, fruity and savoury, a modern style with some vanilla and mocha, and honest value.

**WineAlign community, 2012 vintage: 85 to 88.** Ordinary drinkers were cooler than the critics. Several found it a food wine rather than a sipper. Two thought it flat or short for the money, and one gave it the "not recommended" mark.

**Jancis Robinson, 2020 vintage: score not public.** Andy Howard MW reviewed the 2020, but the score is for members only ([JancisRobinson.com](https://www.jancisrobinson.com/tastings/254935)).

**CellarTracker:** I found no CellarTracker notes for this wine. The only other consumer rating was 4 out of 5 stars from just two reviews of the 2024 at Waitrose.

Overall, professionals agree on about 87–88 points, with one 90 from Falstaff for 2016. Amateur drinkers place it a little lower.

### Practical note

**Check the vintage first.** This wine is built for early drinking, and MacLean's window for the 2013 ended in 2017. A 2019 or later bottle should be fine. If the label says 2012–2016, expect faded fruit; open one before buying more. That would also explain the $6.40 price.

**Drink now.** It is not a cellaring wine.

**Decanting:** not needed. Pouring it into a jug and back is enough to freshen it.

**Temperature:** serve slightly cool, about 14–16 °C. From room temperature, that is roughly 20 minutes in the fridge.

**Dishes:**
- Pork [souvlaki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Souvlaki&go=Go) with lemon and oregano, close to Treve Ring's own suggestion.
- [Moussaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Moussaka&go=Go). The wine's acidity cuts the béchamel.
- [Pastitsio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Pastitsio&go=Go) or a good homemade burger, as MacLean suggests.

### From the history books

- **573 BC: the Nemean Games begin.** From 573 BC the Panhellenic Nemean Games were held at Nemea every two years, rotating with Olympia, Delphi and Isthmia ([Visit Greece](https://www.visitgreece.gr/en/mainland/Peloponnese/nemea)). See [Nemean Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Nemean+Games&go=Go) and the site of [Ancient Nemea](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ancient+Nemea,+Corinthia,+Greece&t=k).
- **Myth: Hercules and the lion.** Legend says [Heracles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Heracles&go=Go) founded the games after his first labour, killing the Nemean lion, which lived in caves on Mount Tritos above the site ([World History Encyclopedia](https://www.worldhistory.org/nemea/.md)). The older myth ties the games to the [Seven Against Thebes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Seven+Against+Thebes&go=Go) and the death of the baby Opheltes.
- **c. 430 BC: free meals for life.** An Athenian law of around 430 BC gave winners at either Nemea or Olympia free meals for life. That shows how highly Nemea was ranked.
- **c. 330 BC: the Temple of Zeus.** The temple of Nemean Zeus was built around 330 BC ([Eagles and Dragons](https://eaglesanddragonspublishing.com/tag/hercules/)). Its columns still stand among the vineyards. See [Temple of Zeus, Nemea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Temple+of+Zeus+Nemea&go=Go).
- **1959 and 2001: the partner winery.** [Evangelos Averoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Evangelos+Averoff&go=Go), a politician and author, planted Greece's first Cabernet Sauvignon on the slopes of the Pindus in the late 1950s, bottling wine in his cellar in Metsovo ([Greek Gastronomy Guide](https://www.greekgastronomyguide.gr/en/item/oinopoieio-katogi-averof-metsovo/)). His winery joined Strofilia in 2001, and Mountain Fish came out of that partnership.

### Curious details

- **"Katogi" means basement.** Averoff first made wine in the *katogi*, the basement of his house ([Wine Odyssey](https://www.wineodyssey.gr/wine-tours-off-the-beaten-path)). The Vlach word for vineyard used in Metsovo, *Gniets*, also survives in the estate's vineyard name ([Greek Gastronomy Guide](https://www.greekgastronomyguide.gr/en/item/oinopoieio-katogi-averof-metsovo/)).
- **Whole-cluster fermentation.** Fermenting whole bunches, stems included, tends to add perfume and lift. It is an unusual choice for a wine at this price ([whole-cluster fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Whole+bunch+fermentation&go=Go); method per [Gismondi on Wine](https://gismondionwine.com/tasting-notes/201705/mountain-fish-agiorgitiko-2014?note=26195)).
- **Altitude in the glass.** At about 800 m, the vines get cooler nights than the valley floor. That keeps the acidity the critics noticed, which helps a warm-climate red stay fresh ([Wine with Seth](https://www.winewithseth.com/winewiki/agiorgitiko/)).
- **A Nemea wine without the Nemea name.** Psari and Asprokambos are inside the Nemea appellation, yet the wine is labelled with the broader PGI Peloponnese. My sources don't explain why.
- **The winners' crown.** Winners at the Nemean Games were crowned with wild celery, a funeral plant linked to the dead child Opheltes. You can see it at the site's museum.

## Ranking by what reviewers say
1. Mountain Fish Red Peloponnese, $6.40 at LCBO [lcbo-392480]: best-supported score 88 points, from Treve Ring (Gismondi on Wine) for the 2014, Natalie MacLean for the 2013, and the WineAlign aggregate for the 2012. Falstaff's 90 for the 2016 is the single highest score.
My own rating is **87/100**. Critics consistently score it at 88, amateurs a little lower, and it is outstanding value at $6.40 if the vintage is still fresh. I've marked it NV because I don't know which vintage is on the shelf.
